item.title: Why your 2-node Proxmox cluster freezes
item.description: With two Proxmox nodes, losing either one leaves the survivor with one vote out of two, so it loses quorum and /etc/pve goes read-only. Here is how a QDevice adds a third vote without a third server, plus the Wi-Fi trap and the emergency lever.
item.content:encoded:
Two Proxmox nodes feel like redundancy. One box dies, the other carries on. That is the picture most people have when they join a second machine to the cluster.

Out of the box, it is the opposite: two machines that can each stop the other from working. This post covers why that happens, the small fix that solves it, and the two related traps that make a cluster look haunted.

How quorum works, in one paragraph

A Proxmox cluster uses Corosync to agree on who is alive. Each node gets one vote, and the cluster is quorate when more than half the votes are present. Without quorum, the cluster filesystem at /etc/pve goes read-only. You can't start guests, change configs or create backups, and nothing in the UI saves.

The trap: 1 vote out of 2 is not a majority

Now do the arithmetic for two nodes. Lose either one, and the survivor holds 1 vote out of 2. That is exactly half, and half is not more than half. So the survivor freezes.

That is the part that catches people. The node that is still up, still powered and still on the network is the one that stops working, because it has no way to know whether the other node is dead or just unreachable. Refusing to write is the safe choice for the cluster, and it is a very annoying choice for you.

You can see the vote count at any time:

pvecm status

The fix: a third vote that isn't a third server

A QDevice is a tiny external voter. It can run on a Raspberry Pi, a NAS container or any always-on Linux box that isn't one of the cluster nodes. It gives the cluster a third vote without a third hypervisor.

With three votes, losing one node leaves 2 out of 3. That is more than half, so the survivor stays quorate and keeps working.

The setup is three installs and one command:

# On the external box (Debian/Ubuntu/Raspberry Pi OS):
apt install corosync-qnetd

# On EVERY cluster node:
apt install corosync-qdevice

# On ONE cluster node (root SSH to the QDevice box must work):
pvecm qdevice setup 192.168.10.5

# Check: you should see 3 total votes and "Qdevice" listed
pvecm status

Replace 192.168.10.5 with the address of your own external box.

Where the QDevice must not live

Don't run the QDevice as a VM or container on one of the cluster nodes. It is tempting, because the hardware is already there. But if that node goes down, it takes its own vote and the QDevice's vote with it, and you are back to 1 vote out of 3 on the survivor. Separate hardware is the whole point.

QDevice placementOne node dies
VM or container on a cluster nodeThat node takes two votes with it; no quorum
Separate always-on boxThe third vote survives; the other node keeps quorum

The related trap: a node on Wi-Fi that keeps flapping

Even with enough votes, a cluster can look broken if one member keeps dropping in and out. The usual cause is Wi-Fi.

Corosync is extremely sensitive to latency and jitter. It wants a stable, low-latency link: single-digit milliseconds, consistently. Wi-Fi delivers great average speeds and terrible consistency. A microwave, a neighbor's channel change or a roaming decision adds 50 to 300 ms of jitter for a few seconds. Corosync sees missed tokens, decides the node is gone, and the cluster reshuffles. A few seconds later it is back. Then it is gone again.

The symptoms look random:

  • The node shows a red X, then turns green again
  • /etc/pve is briefly read-only
  • Backup jobs fail with "cluster not ready"
  • The logs fill with lines like [TOTEM] A processor failed, forming new configuration

Check for it:

journalctl -u corosync --since "24 hours ago" | \
  grep -Ei "failed|new membership|retransmit"
corosync-cfgtool -s        # link status per node
ping -c 100 -i 0.2 <other-node> | tail -2   # look at mdev/max, not avg

Look at the mdev and max numbers from the ping, not the average. A good average with a big max is exactly the jitter Corosync hates.

The fix isn't a Corosync tuning trick. It's a cable. If the node physically can't be wired, use a powerline or MoCA adapter (still better than Wi-Fi), or take it out of the cluster and run it standalone. A standalone node you manage separately is far less trouble than a cluster member that drops out twice an hour.

If your nodes have two network ports, give Corosync a second link (link1) on a separate network or a direct cable between the nodes. Corosync fails over between links automatically.

When you're stuck without quorum right now

If one node of two is dead and you need the survivor working immediately, there is an emergency lever:

pvecm expected 1

This tells the survivor to accept being alone. It is an emergency lever, not a fix. Only use it when you are sure the other node is truly off, because two nodes that each think they are the whole cluster can write conflicting configs. Once the crisis is over, the real fix is still the QDevice.

Scripts: wait for quorum instead of failing halfway

If you script changes on a cluster with a flaky member, check quorum before each write and retry, instead of letting the script die partway through a batch:

until pvecm status | grep -q "Quorate:.*Yes"; do
  echo "waiting for quorum..."; sleep 10
done
pct destroy 123 --purge

The loop waits until pvecm status reports the cluster as quorate, then runs the write. Wrap each destructive or config-changing step this way and a brief membership blip costs you a pause, not a half-finished job.

Checklist

  • Every cluster node is wired, ideally on the same switch
  • Two-node clusters have a QDevice on separate hardware, never on a cluster node
  • pvecm status shows the expected vote count (3 for two nodes plus a QDevice)
  • Corosync logs show no membership changes over the past day
  • Nodes with two ports give Corosync a second link (link1)
  • Scripts check for quorum before each write
  • You know the pvecm expected 1 lever, and when not to pull it

item.title: Grocy Fridge Scanner: update your Grocy stock from a photo
item.description: Take a photo of your fridge or pantry and on-device AI updates your Grocy inventory. No cloud uploads, no account required.
item.content:encoded:
Grocy is a self-hosted tool for tracking what is in your kitchen: stock levels, expiration dates, shopping lists. It is a good fit for a homelab, but it has one weak spot, and anyone who has tried it knows what it is. Keeping it accurate means entering items by hand, and once you fall behind, the inventory stops matching the fridge and the whole system quietly loses its value.

Grocy Fridge Scanner goes after that manual step. You take a photo of your fridge or pantry, an AI model running on your phone identifies what is there, and the app updates your Grocy stock.

What it does

  • Photo scanning. Snap the fridge or pantry, and the on-device model identifies the items in the picture.
  • Automatic counting. Stock levels are counted from the photo instead of typed in.
  • Expiration tracking. The app tracks expiration dates so you know what needs using first.
  • Direct Grocy integration. Updates go straight into your Grocy instance, with real-time inventory sync.
  • Shopping lists. It can generate a shopping list from what you have and what you are missing.
  • Less waste. Knowing what is about to expire is the point, and the listing frames the app around reducing food waste.

How it fits into a Grocy setup

The app sits between your kitchen and the Grocy instance you already run. Instead of opening Grocy and adjusting each product, you take a photo and let the scanner do the identification and counting, then the stock in Grocy is updated for you. The listing's promise is that no manual entry is needed for those updates.

That changes the habit you need to keep the system accurate. Taking a quick photo after a shopping trip, or whenever you open the pantry to plan a meal, is a much smaller ask than typing in every item. A system that is easier to keep up is one that stays accurate, and an accurate Grocy is what makes the expiration tracking and shopping lists worth having.

Who the listing has in mind

The listing names four groups: Grocy users who want automation, anyone tired of manual inventory tracking, families managing household supplies, and minimalists who want to reduce waste. The common thread is that you want the benefits of an inventory without the chore of maintaining one.

Privacy

If you self-host Grocy, there is a good chance you chose it partly to keep household data off someone else's servers. The scanner keeps to the same idea. According to the listing:

  • All processing happens on your device.
  • Photos are not uploaded to the cloud.
  • Your grocery data stays local.
  • No account is required.

Because identification runs on the phone, the photo of the inside of your fridge does not need to go anywhere except into the model on your own device, and the resulting stock changes go to your own Grocy server.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download, with an optional premium upgrade mentioned in the listing.
  • Ads: the app contains ads.
  • Category: Food and Drink, rated Everyone.
  • You need Grocy: the app updates an existing Grocy inventory, so it assumes you already run Grocy or plan to.
  • On-device AI: identification runs locally rather than through a cloud service.

Is it for you?

  • You run Grocy and your stock levels are out of date more often than not.
  • You want expiration dates tracked without logging every item by hand.
  • You manage supplies for a household and want a shopping list built from what is actually there.
  • You prefer that photos of your kitchen stay on your phone.

Get Grocy Fridge Scanner on Google Play

item.title: Never delete this stopped Proxmox VM
item.description: A Proxmox template is always stopped, so it looks exactly like an abandoned VM. Here is how full and linked clones differ, how to find every guest that depends on a base, and how to retire a template safely.
item.content:encoded:
Templates are one of Proxmox's best features. You build a base image once, and new guests come off it in seconds. They are also one of its quietest traps, because they create dependencies you cannot see in the guest list, and those dependencies bite on the day you tidy up.

This post is about that day: what a template really is to the guests built from it, how to prove whether one is load-bearing, and how to retire one without breaking anything.

Full clones vs linked clones

When you clone a template, Proxmox offers two modes:

  • Full clone: a complete, independent copy of the disk. Slower to create, uses more space, depends on nothing.
  • Linked clone: a thin copy that stores only the differences from the template's disk. Instant, tiny, and permanently tied to the template's base disk.

That last part is the whole story. A linked clone is not a copy of the template. It is a layer of changes sitting on top of it. Take away the bottom layer and the top layer has nothing to stand on.

You can see the relationship in the disk names. A template's disks are named like base-9000-disk-0, and a linked clone's config refers to that base, like this:

local-lvm:base-9000-disk-0/vm-105-disk-0

Read it left to right: VM 105's disk lives on top of template 9000's base disk.

The trap: "it's stopped, so it's junk"

Templates are always stopped. In a list of guests, a template looks exactly like an abandoned VM.

There is a nastier version too. A plain stopped container that was converted to a template, then used as the source for linked clones, looks like any other forgotten container. Nothing about it shouts "other guests need me".

Delete that base, and what happens depends on your storage:

StorageWhat happens when you delete the base
ZFS and some othersProxmox refuses, because the base still has dependents
File-based (qcow2 on a directory or NFS)The clones' backing file can simply vanish, and every linked clone built from it stops booting

Either way, you find out at the worst possible moment. The rule of thumb from the book: never delete a template, or anything named base-*, until you have proven nothing references it.

The fix, part 1: find every dependent

Every guest config lives in /etc/pve, so one grep tells you who depends on a base. For template 9000:

# Who uses template 9000's disks?
grep -rl "base-9000-" /etc/pve/nodes/*/qemu-server/ /etc/pve/nodes/*/lxc/

If the grep returns anything other than the template's own config, the template is load-bearing. Leave it, label it, and move on.

To see every template on the cluster in the first place:

# All templates on the cluster
grep -l "^template: 1" /etc/pve/nodes/*/qemu-server/*.conf \
  /etc/pve/nodes/*/lxc/*.conf

The fix, part 2: label the load-bearing guests

The cheapest fix in the whole chapter is a note and a tag. Write it in the guest's Notes field (the Summary tab), and add a keep tag:

qm set 9000 --tags "template,keep" \
  --description "BASE TEMPLATE. Linked clones depend on this. Do not delete."
pct set 9050 --tags "template,keep"

Tags show up as colored pills in the resource tree. A bright red keep tag stops a lot of 1 a.m. mistakes, and the note tells whoever is cleaning up why the guest is there.

The same idea carries into any cleanup script. The book's backup-before-delete loop skips templates outright before it touches anything:

grep -q "^template: 1" /etc/pve/{lxc,qemu-server}/$id.conf 2>/dev/null && \
  { echo "SKIP $id: template"; continue; }

The fix, part 3: untangle before you retire

Sometimes you really do want a template gone: it is old, its OS is out of date, and you have built a better one. You can retire it, but only after its linked clones stop needing it. That means turning each linked clone into a full, independent guest first.

The simplest way is a fresh full clone of each linked clone:

# VM: full, independent copy of linked clone 105 as 305
qm clone 105 305 --full 1 --name app-server
# Container: same idea
pct clone 205 405 --full 1 --hostname app-ct

Moving a disk to a different storage also writes a full copy:

qm disk move 105 scsi0 other-store --delete 1

For containers, pct move-volume does the same job.

Then work through it in order:

  1. Test the full clone.
  2. Retire the linked one.
  3. Rerun the dependents grep for that template.
  4. When it comes back with nothing but the template's own config, the template is finally safe to remove.

Deleting it is still a cleanup like any other: back it up, verify the archive, then destroy with purge.

Long-lived guests should be full clones

Linked clones are instant and tiny, which makes them tempting. But the book's checklist is clear: long-lived production guests should be full clones, so they depend on nothing and a future cleanup cannot pull the floor out from under them.

And because templates stick around, keep them fresh: rebuild or update them on a schedule, with a patched OS and current cloud-init, so new guests do not start life months behind.

Checklist

  • Every template is tagged keep, with a note saying what depends on it
  • You have grepped for base-<id>- before deleting anything that might be a base
  • Any cleanup script skips guests with template: 1 in their config
  • Long-lived production guests are full clones, not linked clones
  • Before retiring a template: full-clone (or disk-move) each linked clone, test it, retire the linked one, rerun the grep
  • Templates are rebuilt or updated on a schedule (patched OS, current cloud-init)

item.title: TrailSage: an offline GPS audio tour guide for your road trips
item.description: TrailSage turns a drive into a guided audio tour, with offline maps and AI commentary generated on your phone. No accounts, no cloud.
item.content:encoded:
Long drives have a way of going quiet in the wrong places. The scenery gets interesting right where the cell signal disappears, and most navigation and tour apps stop being useful at exactly that point. TrailSage is built around the opposite assumption: that you will be somewhere without coverage, and the app should keep working anyway.

It combines offline GPS navigation with an audio tour guide. The commentary is generated by an AI model that runs on the phone itself, so the stories about the places along your route do not depend on a connection or an account.

What it does

  • Offline maps and navigation. You download maps ahead of time, then get turn-by-turn directions and live location tracking without cell service.
  • AI audio tours. An on-device model generates commentary about points of interest along your route, including historical facts and local stories.
  • A choice of voices. The narration comes with multiple voice options.
  • Hands-off playback. Tours can start automatically when you drive, can be paused and resumed, and the narration adjusts to your speed.
  • Trip planning. You can save favorite routes, customize the stops on a tour, share routes with friends, and import GPX files.
  • A driving-friendly interface. The layout is clean, with large buttons and a night mode, and it runs on both phones and tablets.

How a trip with it works

The workflow follows from the feature list. Before you leave, while you still have a connection, you download the maps for the area you are heading into. From there the app does not need the internet: navigation, location tracking and the tour commentary all run on the device.

If you already have a route planned in another tool, the GPX import means you do not have to rebuild it. You can adjust which stops the tour covers, save the route for later, or share it with whoever you are travelling with.

Once you start driving, the auto-start option means the tour can begin without you touching the phone, and the speed-adjusted narration is meant to keep the commentary in step with how fast you are moving. If you stop for fuel or food, you pause and pick it back up later.

Why on-device AI matters here

Generating the tour commentary on the phone is what lets the audio guide work in the same dead zones as the offline maps. A cloud-based guide would go silent the moment the signal dropped. With TrailSage, the model is already on the device, so the stories keep coming.

Privacy

The listing is direct about this. All of the AI processing happens on the device. There is no cloud component and no account to create. Your routes stay on your phone, and the app states that it does no tracking and no data uploads.

For a travel app, that is a meaningful difference. Your route history is a fairly detailed record of where you go, and here it is not leaving the phone.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download, with an optional premium upgrade mentioned in the listing.
  • Ads: the app contains ads.
  • Category: Travel and Local, rated Everyone.
  • Battery: the app is described as battery-efficient, which matters on a long day of navigation.
  • Prepare before you go: offline maps have to be downloaded before you lose service, so do that at home or at your last stop with a connection.

Is it for you?

  • You take road trips through areas where cell coverage is patchy or missing.
  • You want to learn something about the places you are driving past, without reading a screen.
  • You prefer an app that works without an account and keeps your routes on your phone.
  • You already plan routes elsewhere and want to bring them in as GPX files.
  • You want a night mode and large buttons for use in the car.

Get TrailSage: AI Road Trip Guide on Google Play

item.title: Ollama AI Chat: use your Ollama server or offline models on Android
item.description: Ollama AI Chat connects Android to your own Ollama server or runs models like Gemma and Qwen fully on the phone, with optional browser sync.
item.content:encoded:
Running a language model at home is a common homelab project now. Ollama makes it straightforward to host models on your own machine, but you still need a decent way to talk to that server when you are not sitting at your desk. Ollama AI Chat is an Android client for exactly that, and it adds a second mode: running smaller models directly on the phone, with no server at all.

Two ways to run a model

Remote Ollama. Point the app at your home or work Ollama server and you get access to whatever models it hosts. You can add multiple servers, switch models per conversation, and watch responses stream in real time.

On-device. The app can also run models locally through Google's LiteRT-LM runtime. The listing names Gemma 4, Gemma 3, Qwen 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek R1 Distill and Phi-4 Mini, ranging from about 300 MB to about 4 GB depending on capability. You download a model once, and after that chatting works fully offline, with zero network traffic for chat content.

That split is practical. When you are on your home network, the big models on your server are available. When you are somewhere without a connection, a smaller model on the phone still works.

What it does

  • Streaming chat for both remote and on-device models, with history saved locally.
  • Thread organization: pin, archive and label conversations; export or share a whole thread as Markdown.
  • Message tools: copy, share, delete, edit and resend, regenerate, and stop a response mid-stream while keeping what was already written.
  • Search inside a conversation or across all of them, jumping straight to the message.
  • Images for vision-capable remote models, compressed automatically before upload.
  • Voice: speech-to-text input and read-aloud replies.
  • Model control per thread: temperature, top_p, top_k, context window and seed, plus token speed and response time under each reply and full model details (parameters, quantization, template, license).

Web Chat Sync

The newest feature lets you keep chatting from a computer without installing anything on it. You turn on Web Sync in the app's settings and sign in with Google or an email and password. Then you open the web chat page in any desktop or mobile browser, sign in with the same account, and your threads appear.

The interesting part is where the work happens. When you type in the browser, your Android phone receives the message, runs the inference (against your Ollama server or on-device), and streams the answer back to the browser. If the phone is offline, messages queue in the browser and are sent once it reconnects. A presence indicator shows when the phone is online, and the model selector only lists models you have actually installed.

Privacy

Conversation history is stored locally on the device in a Room database. On-device inference sends no chat content over the network. If you turn on Web Sync, threads and messages sync to Firebase Realtime Database under your own account, secured by Firebase Auth, so that part does go through a cloud service. The listing also states there is no third-party advertising data collection for chat content.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download. The app contains ads, and the Play listing notes in-app purchases.
  • Requirements: Android 7.0 (API 24) or higher.
  • Connection: remote Ollama and Web Chat Sync need an internet connection; on-device models work offline after the download.
  • Storage: on-device models take roughly 300 MB to 4 GB each, so check your free space first.
  • Open source: released under the MIT license.

Is it for you?

  • You run an Ollama server and want a proper phone client for it.
  • You want a model that still works on the phone with no connection.
  • You compare models and care about settings like temperature, context window and token speed.
  • You want to continue phone conversations from a browser without installing a desktop app.

Get Ollama AI Chat on Google Play

item.title: OctoPulse: watch and control OctoPrint from your Android phone
item.description: OctoPulse finds OctoPrint on your Wi-Fi, pairs in one tap, and puts progress, camera, temps and controls on your phone. Free, no account.
item.content:encoded:
If you run OctoPrint, you know the routine: a print is going, you have walked away, and now you want to know whether the first layer stuck. Opening the web interface on a phone works, but it was not designed for a small screen. OctoPulse is a native Android companion for OctoPrint that puts the things you check most often (progress, temperatures, the camera) one tap away.

OctoPrint is the open-source web interface many people use to run a 3D printer from a Raspberry Pi or another small computer. OctoPulse talks to it over your network. It works with any printer running OctoPrint, including OctoPi on a Raspberry Pi, and the listing names Ender 3, Prusa and Bambu (with OctoPrint) as examples. The rule of thumb it gives is simple: if you can open OctoPrint in your browser, OctoPulse can connect.

What it does

  • Finds your printer for you. It scans your Wi-Fi using mDNS/Bonjour, SSDP and a subnet scan, so you do not type IP addresses. It also verifies that what it found is really OctoPrint.
  • Pairs without copying API keys. It uses OctoPrint's official Application Keys: tap the printer, approve the request in OctoPrint, and it is connected.
  • Shows every printer on one dashboard. Status, progress percentage, time remaining, and nozzle and bed temperatures, with pull to refresh.
  • Streams the camera. MJPEG or snapshot streaming, with flip, rotate and automatic reconnect.
  • Gives you real control. Jog X, Y and Z, home the axes, extrude and retract, set temperatures, run the fan, hit emergency stop, or send G-code from a terminal.
  • Previews G-code. A 2D and 3D layer viewer with pinch-zoom and orbit.
  • Manages files. Browse what is on OctoPrint, see details, start a print or delete a file.
  • Sends alerts. Notifications when a print finishes or fails, and at 25, 50, 75 and 90 percent, with per-printer toggles and background polling. It respects Do Not Disturb.

Getting started

The setup the listing describes is three steps:

  1. Install OctoPulse and join the same Wi-Fi network as your OctoPrint server.
  2. Tap Discover Printers on Wi-Fi, choose your printer, tap Pair, and approve the request inside OctoPrint.
  3. From there you can monitor progress, watch the camera, pause or stop if needed, and start the next print.

For access away from home, OctoPulse does not provide its own cloud relay. Instead you point it at your VPN or reverse proxy URL, and OctoPrint has to be reachable that way.

Privacy and permissions

This is where OctoPulse fits a self-hosted setup well. There is no account and no sign-up. Print files, G-code and camera feeds do not go to the developer's servers; the data stays between your phone and your printer. Hosts, API keys and camera URLs are encrypted on the device, with the keys stored using the Android Keystore.

The permissions are limited to what the features need: network and Wi-Fi state, multicast for mDNS discovery, notifications for print alerts, starting at boot to reschedule alerts, vibration, and the advertising ID for ads. It does not request location, camera or contacts. Discovery scans your local subnet only.

Good to know

  • Price: free, with no subscription.
  • Ads: it contains ads, a small banner plus an occasional full-screen ad after setup steps. The listing says ads are never shown during a print.
  • Open source: the app is released under the MIT license.
  • Look and feel: dark theme, haptics and offline handling.
  • Not official: OctoPulse is not affiliated with the OctoPrint project.

Is it for you?

  • You already run OctoPrint, on a Raspberry Pi or another machine.
  • You want progress, temps and the camera on your phone without opening a browser.
  • You run more than one printer and want them on a single dashboard.
  • You would rather keep printer data on your own network than in someone's cloud.
  • You already have a VPN or reverse proxy if you want to check prints remotely.

Get OctoPulse: OctoPrint Companion on Google Play

item.title: RAID is not a backup: the 3-2-1 rule, honestly
item.description: What actually counts as a copy under the 3-2-1 rule, why a RAID mirror or a snapshot only protects against one kind of failure, and the one-page inventory that exposes the gaps.
item.content:encoded:
Three copies of anything you care about, on two different kinds of storage, with one of them somewhere else. Everyone has heard the 3-2-1 rule. Far fewer homelabs actually have it, because the rule is easy to say and the details are where it falls apart.

The problem is usually not that people have no backups. It is that some of the copies they are counting are not copies at all.

Things that feel like backups but aren't

RAID or a ZFS mirror. That is one copy on resilient disks. It protects you from a dead drive and from nothing else: not from rm -rf, not from a bad update, not from ransomware, not from the host catching fire. Delete a file and the mirror faithfully deletes it on both disks.

Snapshots. A ZFS or Proxmox snapshot lives on the same pool as the data. It is a wonderful undo button and a terrible backup. Lose the pool and the snapshots go with it.

A second copy on the same box. vzdump writing to a different directory on the same host is one disk failure away from losing both copies.

The NAS. A copy on the NAS is a real second copy. It is still in the same house, on the same power circuit, behind the same door.

The cloud sync folder. Sync is not backup. Delete the file at home and the cloud deletes it too, sometimes with a short grace period, sometimes not.

What actually counts

A copy counts when it survives the loss of the thing it was copied from. That one sentence settles most arguments about what is and isn't a backup.

Two kinds of storage means two things that do not fail together: local disk and a NAS, local disk and object storage, a Proxmox Backup Server datastore and a tape if you are that kind of person.

Off-site means a different building. A friend's house across town is off-site. The garage is not.

A shape that satisfies the rule for a typical Proxmox homelab looks like this:

CopyWhereProtects against
1. The live dataProxmox hosts, ZFS mirrorsA dead disk (and nothing else)
2. Nightly backupsProxmox Backup Server on a separate box, plus vzdump to the NAS for a few guestsMistakes, bad updates, a dead host
3. Off-siteEncrypted copy in object storage, or a PBS sync to a friend's boxFire, theft, flood, ransomware that reaches the NAS

Notice that row 1 is in the table. The live data is a copy, it just is not a backup. RAID earns its place by keeping you running through a disk failure, not by protecting your history.

Write the inventory first

Before touching a single backup job, write down what you are protecting. It fits on one page and it is one of the most useful documents a homelab can have.

One row per thing, four columns:

  1. What it is (Home Assistant VM, OPNsense, the photo server, the Proxmox hosts themselves, the NAS data share)
  2. How it is backed up
  3. How far back you can go
  4. How you would restore it

The last column is the one that exposes the holes. It is easy to write "nightly backup" in column two. It is much harder to write a restore path you have actually tried. Any row with "none" in column two, or a restore path you have never tested, is your to-do list.

Keep the table somewhere that survives the homelab: a note on your phone or a printed page. A recovery plan stored only on the server you are recovering is not much of a plan.

Decide what you do not back up

Backing up everything is how backup storage fills up and jobs start failing. Some things are cheaper to rebuild than to store:

  • Downloaded ISOs and container templates. Keep a list, not the files.
  • Media libraries you can re-rip or re-download, if you are honest about whether you would.
  • Scratch VMs and test containers. Tag them scratch so the exclude is obvious.
  • Caches: transcodes, thumbnails an app will regenerate, package caches.

Everything not on that list gets backed up by default. "By default" is the important phrase: a backup job that protects new guests automatically, rather than a hand-picked list, is what makes it true.

Checklist

  • Inventory written: one row per thing, with how it is backed up, how far back, and the restore path
  • Every row has a copy on a second kind of storage and one off-site
  • RAID, snapshots and sync folders are not counted as backups anywhere in the table
  • A short list of what you deliberately do not back up, and why
  • The table lives somewhere that survives the homelab

RAID keeps you running. Backups get you back. You want both, and you want to know which one you are looking at.

Go deeper: Never Lose Your Data

item.title: Proxmox backups that actually work: 3-2-1, step by step
item.description: The whole backup playbook in one walk-through: the 3-2-1 plan, vzdump, Proxmox Backup Server, retention, an off-site copy, restore drills and the alert for jobs that quietly stop.
item.content:encoded:
Your Proxmox backup job has a schedule, a storage target and a little green check. That check proves one thing: the job wrote some bytes somewhere. It does not prove every guest is covered, that the copy survives a dead host, or that anything actually restores.

This post walks through a complete homelab backup setup in the order you would build it, one layer at a time. Each layer closes a hole the previous one leaves open.

1. The plan: 3-2-1, honestly

Three copies of anything you care about, on two different kinds of storage, with one of them somewhere else.

A copy only counts if it survives the loss of the thing it was copied from. That rules out RAID and ZFS mirrors (one copy on resilient disks), snapshots (same pool as the data), a second copy on the same host, and sync folders (delete at home, delete in the cloud). The NAS is a real second copy, but it is still in the same house. Off-site means a different building.

Before touching any job, write a one-page inventory: each thing you run, how it is backed up, how far back you can go, and how you would restore it. The restore column is the one that exposes the gaps.

2. vzdump: the backup you already have

Every Proxmox install ships with vzdump. Point it at storage that is not the host's own disk, such as an NFS share on the NAS:

pvesm add nfs nas-backup --server 192.168.10.40 --export /volume1/proxmox \
  --content backup --options vers=4.1

Then create one job under Datacenter → Backup → Add with Selection mode: All and your scratch guests under Exclude, so every new guest is protected the day it is created. Snapshot mode, ZSTD compression, a nightly schedule and a notes template like {{guestname}} on {{node}}.

Install the QEMU guest agent in every VM and enable it in the VM's Options. With it, snapshot mode asks the guest to flush its filesystems first, which is the difference between a consistent backup and one that needs fsck on restore.

3. Proxmox Backup Server: when vzdump isn't enough

PBS adds deduplication, incremental backups, verify jobs and client-side encryption. The trap is running it on the same host, or in a VM on the same host with its datastore on the same pool. It works beautifully until the host dies, and then the backups die with it. Give PBS its own hardware, however modest: an old office PC with one large disk and 4 GB of RAM is plenty for a home datastore.

Connect it with a dedicated backup@pbs user rather than root, and turn on client-side encryption:

pvesm set pbs01 --encryption-key autogen

Every chunk is then encrypted before it leaves the node. Download that key immediately and store it somewhere that is not the cluster, such as a password manager or a printed QR code. Without the key, every encrypted backup is unrecoverable. Losing it is the one mistake with no undo.

Running both is a sensible shape: PBS nightly for everything, plus vzdump to the NAS for the few guests you want as single portable files.

4. Retention that lets you sleep

keep-daily=7 does not mean "keep seven days". It means "keep the last backup from each of the last seven days that have a backup". If the job failed for a month and then ran once, that one run can satisfy every keep rule at once, and pruning deletes the older history. The rules keep the newest backup per calendar bucket; they never promise coverage of time.

Retention also does not protect you from a bad backup: if the guest was already corrupted, you just have seven copies of the corruption. That is why weekly and monthly buckets matter. Set retention on the storage or the PBS prune job, not per job, check it in the prune simulator, and take a protected backup before every risky change so pruning cannot touch it.

5. Off-site: the copy that survives the house

Three realistic options: an encrypted copy in Backblaze B2 via rclone, a PBS sync job to a friend's box over Tailscale, or a USB disk rotated to work. The USB disk is cheap and fast to restore from, but it is not automatic, and that is its problem.

For B2, put an rclone crypt remote on top of the bucket with a key scoped to that bucket, sync the dump directory nightly with a bandwidth limit during the day, add a lifecycle rule so hidden versions expire, and run rclone check monthly. Store the two crypt passwords with your PBS key, outside the homelab. And read the current B2 price from Backblaze's own pricing page rather than from any guide, including this one.

The trap here is the off-site copy that was set up once and never checked: an expired app key, a friend's box that was powered off, a bucket that filled up. Off-site is where "no news is good news" does the most damage.

6. Restore testing: the only proof

"Verified" means different things at each layer. A job reporting OK means it finished writing. zstd -t means the archive is complete and decompresses. A PBS verify job means the chunks still match their hashes. None of them means the guest boots.

Once a quarter, run four drills, each restored to a new ID with the network unplugged, then destroyed:

  1. A VM from PBS. Does it boot, and is last night's data there?
  2. A container from a vzdump archive on the NAS (second tool, second storage).
  3. A single file from PBS using File Restore. This is the restore you will do most often.
  4. Something from off-site. This is the only drill that proves the copy that survives the house.
qmrestore pbs01:backup/vm/101/2026-10-08T01:30:00Z 9101 \
  --storage local-zfs --unique 1
qm set 9101 --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0,link_down=1
qm start 9101

Write each drill down: date, what, from where, result. A drill nobody wrote down did not happen.

7. Alerts for the jobs that quietly stop

Alerting only on failure has a blind spot: a job that never runs never fails. The alert you need is "nothing succeeded recently".

Use the Proxmox notification system (VE 8.1+) for warnings and errors, then add a dead-man's switch: a check URL, from a service like healthchecks.io or a self-hosted Uptime Kuma push monitor, that your job pings on success. vzdump's hook script makes it a few lines in /etc/vzdump.conf. Set the check's period to a day with a grace of a few hours, and a night the job does not run becomes a phone notification by breakfast. Do the same for the rclone sync.

Finally, a weekly backup-age report that lists the newest backup of every guest and flags any older than two days, or any guest with no backup at all. That catches the "selected VMs" trap no matter how it sneaks back in.

The short version

  • An inventory with a tested restore path per row
  • One vzdump or PBS job in Selection mode All, on storage that is not the host
  • PBS on its own hardware, encrypted, key saved outside the cluster
  • Retention you have actually checked in the simulator
  • An off-site copy that is automatic and monitored
  • Quarterly restore drills, written down
  • A dead-man's switch, so silence becomes an alert

Go deeper: Never Lose Your Data

item.title: Your Proxmox backup job is probably skipping your new VMs
item.description: A backup job built for a hand-picked list of guests silently misses every VM you create afterwards. Here is how to switch to "All" with excludes, and the other checks that make the green tick mean something.
item.content:encoded:
Open your Proxmox web UI, click your backup storage and sort by date. Is there a backup of every guest you care about from the last 48 hours? For a lot of homelabs the honest answer is "most of them", and "most" is how data gets lost.

A backup job in the Datacenter view looks reassuring. It has a schedule, a storage target and a little green check. That check proves one thing: the job wrote some bytes somewhere. It does not prove that every guest you care about is in there.

The trap: a job built for "selected VMs"

The most common way this goes wrong is the selection mode. Somebody (often past you) created the job for "selected VMs" when the homelab had five guests. Every guest built after that day is unprotected, and the job keeps reporting success every night, because the guests it knows about are fine.

Nothing errors. Nothing emails you. The list of protected guests and the list of running guests just drift apart, one new container at a time.

The fix: one job that covers everything

Make your main job cover all guests, and exclude the few you truly do not want. New guests are protected the day they are created. If you only make one change after reading this, make this one.

In the UI: Datacenter → Backup → Add, then:

  • Selection mode: All, with scratch and test guests under Exclude.
  • Mode: Snapshot for running guests. The guest keeps running. Stopped guests are backed up too; Proxmox just reads their disks, and the forgotten stopped VM is often the one you will want back.
  • Compression: ZSTD. Fast and small.
  • Schedule: nightly, at a time nobody is using anything, for example 02:30.
  • Retention: "use storage defaults", so the numbers live in one place.
  • Notes template: {{guestname}} on {{node}}, so the backup list is readable when a VM ID means nothing to you at 2 AM.

The same job from the command line, if you like to keep config in version control:

pvesh create /cluster/backup \
  --schedule "02:30" \
  --all 1 \
  --storage nas-backup \
  --mode snapshot \
  --compress zstd \
  --notes-template "{{guestname}} on {{node}}"

Need to leave out a scratch VM? Use --exclude 9001,9002 instead of switching back to selected guests. An exclude list fails safe; an include list fails dangerous. If you forget to update an exclude list, you back up one guest too many. If you forget to update an include list, you lose a guest.

Three other things hiding behind the green check

The selection mode is the big one, but it is not the only way a "working" job quietly stops protecting you.

1. The storage silently isn't there

If your NAS is added as a plain Directory storage on a path you mounted yourself, and that mount fails at boot, Proxmox will happily write backups into the empty folder on your root disk. A night or two later the host's root filesystem is full and things break in confusing ways.

Either use the native NFS storage type, which lets Proxmox manage the mount and mark the storage offline if it fails, or tell Proxmox the path must be a mountpoint:

pvesm set nas-backup --is_mountpoint yes

And check before you trust it:

pvesm status                 # every storage should say "active"
df -h /mnt/pve/nas-backup    # should show the NAS size, not the root disk

2. Nobody gets told

By default, failures go to the root mailbox on the host, which nobody reads. Proxmox VE 8.1 and later has a proper notification system under Datacenter → Notifications. Add a target you actually read, point backup events at it, and set the job's notification mode to use it. Then test it on purpose:

vzdump 101 --storage does-not-exist

If no alert arrives, fix that before anything else. A weekly "all good" message is worth having too: silence is ambiguous, and a success message that suddenly stops arriving is a signal.

3. Nothing gets pruned

Without retention, the backup share fills up and every job after that fails. Set retention on the storage itself so every job that writes there inherits it:

pvesm set nas-backup \
  --prune-backups keep-last=2,keep-daily=7,keep-weekly=4,keep-monthly=3

Those numbers do not mean what most people think they mean. That is a post of its own.

Prove it: a backup you haven't restored is a rumor

A green check says the job finished writing. A quick integrity check says the archive is readable end to end:

zstd -t /mnt/pve/nas-backup/dump/vzdump-qemu-101-*.vma.zst

Only a restore proves the guest actually comes back. Restore to a spare ID, with the network disconnected so it does not fight the original for an IP, boot it, look around, then destroy the test copy:

qmrestore /mnt/pve/nas-backup/dump/vzdump-qemu-101-<date>.vma.zst 9101 \
  --storage local-zfs --unique 1

--unique gives the restored VM fresh MAC addresses so it can sit next to the original.

Checklist

  • One backup job set to All guests (with excludes), not a hand-picked list
  • Backup storage is native NFS or PBS, or has is_mountpoint set
  • Retention set on the storage
  • Failure notifications reach somewhere you actually read, and you have tested them
  • The newest backup of every guest is less than 48 hours old
  • One test restore done, to a new ID, and written down with the date

Five minutes in the Datacenter view now is a lot cheaper than finding out during a restore that the VM you need was never in the job.

Go deeper: Never Lose Your Data

item.title: The one wire that can fry your ESP32 tank monitor
item.description: A turbidity sensor runs on 5 V and outputs up to about 4.5 V, but an ESP32-C3's pins only take 3.3 V. Here is why it needs a voltage divider, how to wire it, and the checks to do before you plug in USB.
item.content:encoded:
A water-quality monitor for an aquarium or turtle tank is a great first ESP32 project: a temperature probe, a TDS probe and a turbidity (water clarity) sensor, all reporting into Home Assistant. Two of those three sensors are easy. The third one has a wire that can kill the board if it goes in the wrong place.

This walkthrough uses the Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3, the board used in the Smart Turtle Tank build, but the rule applies to any 3.3 V microcontroller.

The rule that keeps the board alive

Two voltages come out of the XIAO:

  • 5V is the USB supply passed straight through.
  • 3V3 is regulated down for the chip.

The chip's pins can only take 3.3 V on their inputs. So the rule is simple: a sensor's power can come from 5V if it needs it, but anything that goes back into a D pin must be at or under 3.3 V.

The DS18B20 temperature probe and the TDS board both run happily on 3.3 V and produce signals under 3.3 V. The turbidity board is the odd one out: it needs 5 V to run and its output can reach about 4.5 V. That is the wire that can fry your board, and it is why the turbidity sensor is the one with a voltage divider between it and the XIAO.

A common mistake is plugging a sensor into 5V "because it is more power". The TDS board and the temperature adapter are powered from 3.3 V precisely so their signal pins stay under the XIAO's limit. More volts in means more volts out.

What the divider does

A voltage divider is two resistors in series. The output is taken from across the smaller one, so the voltage is split in a fixed ratio. The divider module used in this build divides by 5, so a 4.5 V signal comes out at 0.9 V: safe for the pin.

The trade-off is detail. The XIAO reads analog accurately only up to about 2.5 V, and 0.9 V uses about a third of that range. For more resolution you can swap in two 10 kΩ resistors as a ÷2 divider, which keeps the output under 2.25 V. Either way, you multiply the reading by the ratio (5 or 2) in code.

The divider module's labels confuse almost everyone the first time:

Label on the moduleWhat it actually is
VCC screw terminalThe input (IN+)
GND screw terminalIN−
S pinThe divided output
− pinGround

Wiring the turbidity sensor

Keep the USB-C cable unplugged the whole time you wire. It goes in last.

Part 1: power the sensor and feed its signal into the divider

  1. Slide the switch on the turbidity board to A (analog), not D.
  2. Plug the included 3-wire cable into the board, and connect the probe.
  3. Red jumper from the XIAO's 5V pin to the cable's V pin. This is the only 5V wire in the build, and it skips the breadboard power strip.
  4. Cable's G wire into the ground (−) rail.
  5. Cable's S wire into the divider's VCC screw terminal (the input). Tighten it and give it a gentle tug.

Part 2: ground the divider and send its safe signal to D2

  1. Ground jumper from the − rail to the divider's GND terminal.
  2. Ground jumper from the − rail to the divider's − pin.
  3. Signal jumper from the divider's S pin to the XIAO's D2.
  4. Leave the divider's + pin empty.

Only the clear lower part of the probe goes in the water. The top of the probe and every board stay dry.

Never plug the turbidity S pin straight into the XIAO.

Check everything before you power up

With the USB still unplugged, go through this list:

  • The turbidity switch is on A.
  • The 3V3 (+) rail has three wires: XIAO 3V3, temperature adapter VCC, TDS +. Nothing from 5V.
  • Only one wire on 5V, going to the turbidity board's V.
  • Turbidity S goes to the divider, not to the XIAO. D2 connects to the divider's S pin.
  • Signals: D4 to the temperature adapter's DAT, D1 to the TDS board's A, D2 to the divider's S.
  • No bare metal touching anything it should not. Every board is dry and above the water line.
  • Each cable hangs in a small U-shaped drip loop below the electronics, so water runs off the bottom of the loop instead of into the boards.

Then plug in USB. Nothing should get warm and nothing should smell; if it does, unplug right away and recheck the 5V and GND wires.

Another common mistake: plugging the USB in "just to see the light" halfway through wiring. Every wire you add after that goes onto a live board, and a jumper that brushes 5V against a signal pin on its way in can take out the whole board. USB last, every time.

Two readings that tell you something is wrong

Once firmware is loaded, temperature should show a sensible number, TDS reads near zero in air and a steady number in the tank, and turbidity reads higher in clear water and drops when the water gets cloudy.

Two problems catch almost everyone:

  • The temperature reads 85 °C. That is the DS18B20's power-on value, which means it never got a successful read. It is usually a loose DAT wire.
  • Turbidity is flat no matter what the water does. The board's switch was left on D (digital) instead of A.

Get the one 5V wire right, put the divider in the turbidity signal path, and plug in USB last. The rest of the build is forgiving.

item.title: keep-daily=7 doesn't mean 7 days of backups
item.description: Proxmox and PBS retention keeps the newest backup in each calendar bucket, not a span of days. How a month of failed jobs can prune away your history, how the keep-* rules combine, and how to set retention in one place.
item.content:encoded:
Retention answers one question: how far back can you go? Most homelabs set it once, glance at keep-daily=7, and assume they have a week of history. That assumption is the trap.

The answer to "how far back" should come from your inventory of what you protect, not from how much disk you happen to have. And it starts with reading the keep-* options correctly.

The trap: buckets, not days

keep-daily=7 does not mean "keep seven days." It means "keep the last backup from each of the last seven days that have a backup."

That last part is the whole problem. Picture a job that fails quietly for a month and then runs once. That one good run satisfies keep-daily, keep-weekly and keep-monthly all at once, and pruning happily deletes the older backups. The rules keep the most recent backup for each calendar bucket; they never promise coverage of time.

So a retention policy that looks like three months of history on paper can collapse to a single backup, with no error anywhere, if the jobs stop running.

The second trap: retention doesn't fix a bad backup

Retention does not protect you from a backup that was bad when it was taken. If the guest was already corrupted when the backup ran, you now have seven pristine copies of corruption.

Retention is about reaching back past the moment something went wrong. That is why the weekly and monthly buckets matter more than the daily ones: a slow corruption can take weeks to notice, and by then the dailies have all rolled over.

How the rules combine

Each rule runs independently, and a backup survives if any rule claims it. That means you can tune the depth per type of guest instead of using one set of numbers for everything. The book's combination looks like this:

Guest typekeep-lastdailyweeklymonthlyWhy
Databases, Home Assistant, Immich21486A slow corruption can take weeks to notice
Ordinary services2743Mistakes get noticed inside a week
OPNsense2086It barely changes; config.xml covers the rest
vzdump copies on the NAS1042Full copies are big; PBS has the depth

keep-last is the safety margin. It protects the newest backups even if they fall on the same day as a pruned one, and it covers the "you just took a backup before an upgrade" case.

Before you commit to any numbers, open the Prune Simulator in the Proxmox Backup Server docs (search for "Prune Simulator") and check what actually survives on a calendar. Proxmox's own retention example in the vzdump docs walks through the same thing and is worth reading once.

The fix: set it in one place

Retention belongs on the storage, not on each job. For a vzdump storage such as an NFS share, set it on the storage so every job that writes there inherits it:

pvesm set nas-backup \
  --prune-backups keep-last=2,keep-daily=7,keep-weekly=4,keep-monthly=3

For Proxmox Backup Server, retention lives in the datastore's prune job, and you can give different namespaces or groups different rules. Set the same keep-* numbers there that you chose for each guest type.

On the backup jobs themselves, leave Retention on "use storage defaults". Setting retention on a job as well gives you two sets of rules fighting each other.

On PBS, remember that pruning only unlinks the index. Garbage collection is what actually frees chunks, and only chunks older than a grace period (24 hours and 5 minutes by default). Schedule GC daily and expect free space to lag pruning by a day.

Changing the numbers later

Changing retention is safe in one direction only. Raising the numbers keeps more. Lowering them deletes on the next prune, with no undo.

If you are short on space, run the change through the simulator first, and if something has to give, shorten the vzdump retention, not the PBS one.

Protected backups for risky changes

Before any change you might regret, such as a major Home Assistant upgrade, a Proxmox major version, or migrating a database, take a manual backup and mark it protected. A protected backup survives every prune until you remove the flag.

In the Proxmox GUI, select the backup and tick Protected. On the command line:

V=pbs01:backup/vm/101/2026-10-04T01:30:00Z
pvesh set /nodes/pve1/storage/pbs01/content/$V --protected 1

Make a habit of clearing them after a month. Protected backups do not count toward keep-*, so they pile up.

How much space to plan for

Real numbers depend on your data, but the book gives a sizing rule of thumb for a new PBS disk: the first backup of a guest is roughly its used disk space after compression, and each further day adds about the daily change. For the book's mix of guests, a year of PBS history fits in about twice the live data.

For vzdump full copies, multiply the guest's used size by the number of copies you keep, then add a third for growth.

Checklist: retention

  • Keep-* numbers chosen per guest type from your inventory, not from free space
  • Checked in the prune simulator that a month of failed jobs cannot wipe your history
  • Retention set on the storage or the PBS prune job, with jobs on "use storage defaults"
  • PBS garbage collection scheduled daily
  • A protected backup taken before every risky change, and cleared a month later
  • Backup storage sized with room for a year of growth

Retention only keeps history if backups keep landing. A month of silent failures is exactly what turns keep-daily=7 into a single copy, so pair these numbers with an alert for jobs that stop running.

Go deeper: Never Lose Your Data

item.title: Delete old Proxmox VMs without regret
item.description: The backup, verify, then destroy-with-purge routine for clearing out stopped guests safely, including the linked-clone check that stops you deleting something a running VM depends on.
item.content:encoded:
Every homelab accumulates guests. The container you built to try something, the VM from a tutorial, the old version of a service you migrated away from. Eventually most of the guest list is grey stopped icons, and the nightly backup job is dutifully copying all of them.

Cleaning house is easy to put off because deleting things is scary. The way to make it not scary is a routine where every single guest you delete is recoverable: back it up, verify the backup, then destroy with purge.

The trap: stopped is not the same as unused

A template is always stopped. A container that was turned into the base of linked clones is always stopped. Delete the base and the clones keep running until the next reboot, and then they do not.

So before you delete anything, find out what is actually unused.

Step 0: check for linked clones

For every stopped guest, check whether any config references its disks as a base:

for id in $(pct list | awk 'NR>1 && $2=="stopped"{print $1}') \
          $(qm list | awk 'NR>1 && $3=="stopped"{print $1}'); do
  if grep -lq "base-${id}-" /etc/pve/nodes/*/*/*.conf 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "KEEP $id: base for linked clones"
  else
    echo "candidate $id"
  fi
done

Tag anything marked KEEP as keep in the GUI and it is out of the discussion. Then walk the candidates with a human eye: the name, the notes, the last-modified date of its config. If you are not sure what a guest is, start it, look, stop it. Ten minutes per mystery guest is cheaper than one wrong destroy.

Step 1: back it up, in stop mode

A stopped guest does not need snapshot mode, and stop mode gives the most consistent archive. Write it to your backup storage with vzdump so the result is one portable file, and give it a note that will mean something in a year:

vzdump 212 --storage nas-backup --mode stop --compress zstd --bwlimit 60000 \
  --notes-template 'DELETED {{guestname}} ({{vmid}}) cleanup 2026-10'

Watch the backup storage's free space as you go. Work in order of "would be saddest to lose", and if the share gets tight, prune old nightly backups to make room before carrying on. The bandwidth limit keeps your busy guests from lagging while the dumps run; it costs a few minutes per guest.

Step 2: verify the archive

A backup you have not at least integrity-checked is a rumour. For a container archive:

zstd -t /mnt/pve/nas-backup/dump/vzdump-lxc-212-2026_10_09-21_14_03.tar.zst

VM archives are .vma.zst files and the same zstd -t works. This proves the file is whole and decompresses. It does not prove the guest boots. For anything you would truly mourn, go further: restore it to a new ID and start it with the network unplugged.

Then mark the archive protected, so the nightly prune cannot eat it:

F=vzdump-lxc-212-2026_10_09-21_14_03.tar.zst
pvesh set /nodes/pve1/storage/nas-backup/content/nas-backup:backup/$F \
  --protected 1

Step 3: destroy, with purge

pct destroy 212 --purge
# or
qm destroy 212 --purge

--purge removes the guest from every backup job, the replication config and HA. Without it, the nightly backup job keeps a reference to a guest that no longer exists and fails with an error about that ID every night until you edit the job by hand.

The loop

For more than a handful of guests, put the IDs in a file (one per line, after the human pass) and let a script do the three steps:

#!/bin/bash
set -u
STORE=nas-backup
DUMP=/mnt/pve/$STORE/dump
NOTE="DELETED {{guestname}} ({{vmid}}) cleanup $(date +%Y-%m)"
while read -r id; do
  if pct config "$id" >/dev/null 2>&1; then kind=lxc; cmd=pct
  else kind=qemu; cmd=qm; fi
  echo "== $id ($kind)"
  vzdump "$id" --storage $STORE --mode stop --compress zstd \
    --bwlimit 60000 --notes-template "$NOTE" \
    || { echo "backup FAILED $id"; continue; }
  f=$(ls -t $DUMP/vzdump-$kind-$id-*.zst | head -1)
  zstd -t "$f" || { echo "verify FAILED $id"; continue; }
  vol="$STORE:backup/$(basename "$f")"
  pvesh set /nodes/$(hostname)/storage/$STORE/content/$vol --protected 1
  $cmd destroy "$id" --purge || echo "destroy FAILED $id (retry later)"
done < /root/cleanup-ids.txt

Every continue means a failure leaves the guest in place. Nothing is ever destroyed without a verified archive ahead of it.

Two gotchas

Cluster quorum. On a two-node cluster, if one node drops off, destroys on the cluster fail with a quorum error while it is out. Re-run the failed IDs once the cluster is quorate again. The proper fix is a QDevice, so the cluster has a third vote.

Leftover locks. Proxmox will not back up or destroy a guest while a lock from an earlier interrupted job is set. pct unlock 212 or qm unlock 212 clears it, once you have checked nothing is actually running against the guest.

Afterwards: the orphans

With the guests gone, there is a second layer of junk:

  • Orphan disks: entries in pvesm list local-zfs that no config references. Compare against grep -h 'local-zfs:' /etc/pve/nodes/*/*/*.conf. Back each one up as a raw image before removing it, same rule.
  • Old ISOs and container templates in local. They download again in minutes.
  • Year-old snapshots on running guests (qm listsnapshot <id>, pct listsnapshot <id>). A snapshot that old is a backup you forgot, on the same disk as the data, slowing every write.

Checklist

  • Every stopped guest checked for linked clones (base-<id>- in any config); templates tagged keep
  • A stop-mode vzdump of each candidate with a "DELETED" note, bandwidth-limited
  • zstd -t on every archive, and the archive marked protected
  • destroy --purge, never plain destroy
  • Failed steps leave the guest in place
  • Orphan disks, old ISOs and year-old snapshots cleaned in a second pass
